utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the Registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-PT, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May we have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning afternoon, Your Honours, counsel and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of the accused, Mr. Rasim Delic, this afternoon, Stephane Bourgon, lawyer from Montreal, Canada, accompanied this afternoon by Ms. Jasenka Residovic, legal assistant. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I am told we also have the Minister of Justice of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ms. Kristo Borjana. Thank you for coming. This is a provisional release application pursuant to Rule 65. The Chamber has had the benefit of reading all the submissions. We have read them very carefully. Accordingly, the submissions to be made in court need not be very long. For that reason, each party will have 20 minutes to make their submissions. And I'll start with counsel for the accused, Mr. Bourgon. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Mr. President, as the Chamber has highlighted, this is an oral hearing which has to do with a motion for provisional release of the accused, Rasim Delic, pursuant to Rule 65 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Mr. President, I will agree with you that one, my submissions this afternoon need not be very long because most of our arguments are already on the record. However, Mr. President, as you may well understand, this is a very important day for any accused, accused before this Tribunal in terms of having the opportunity to address the Court and to be heard with respect to provisional release. I will begin, quickly, Mr. President, by simply highlighting a couple of general facts of this case which includes that the indictment against Mr. Delic was confirmed on the 16th of February; that Mr. Delic immediately notified the authorities of his willingness to surrender and to be transferred in the custody of the International Tribunal; and that his transfer was immediately organised as early as 28th of February, with and in cooperation with the government of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as the Office of the Prosecution. Since being transferred in the custody of the International Tribunal, Mr. Delic has been at the United Nations Detention Unit, where he has been -- he had good conduct and there were no problems whatsoever with respect to his staying at the UNDU. Mr. Delic had his initial appearance on the 3rd of March at which time he pleaded not guilty to every charge in the indictment. Mr. President, our case this afternoon is quite straightforward. The two conditions which are found in Rule 65(B) are met and there are, in our view, no other specific and objective reasons which outweigh the need to ensure respect for the right of liberty of the accused. Now, as we know, Mr. President, these conditions are that Mr. Delic, if granted provisional release, will return for his trial, and that he will not pose a danger to any victim. I will focus, Mr. President, on two issues: the guarantees provided by the government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as the personal situation of Rasim Delic. First, with respect to the guarantees which have been provided by the government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. These guarantees were provided in writing on the 3rd of March, 2005. Those guarantees are provided by the Federation which, in accordance with the Rules, is an entity and is able to provide the required guarantees. The guarantees provided by the Federation include the guarantee to carry out any orders which could be issued by this Trial Chamber or by any other Chamber of the International Tribunal. I highlight the fact this afternoon, Mr. President, I am accompanied by the Minister of Justice of the Federation, Ms. Borjana Kristo. She will be able, Mr. President, at your request, to highlight the cooperation which has been given by the government of the Federation, with -- to the International Tribunal. When we speak of cooperation, Mr. President, we need to think of two things. The record of cooperation is general cooperation with the Tribunal, as any state is obligated to cooperate with the Tribunal. In this respect the record of the Federation has been very good. Of course, cooperation is also meaning in relation to other accused who have been provisionally released in the past. A number of accused have indeed been released, and -- for whom the Federation has provided guarantees, guarantees which include that not only will they carry out orders issued by the Tribunal, but should there be any attempt or any indication that an accused put on provisional release wanted to escape or did not respect any of the conditions imposed by this Trial Chamber, the government of the Federation would immediately intervene. I believe the Minister of Justice, Mr. President, will be in a better position than I am to provide and to explain in a more specific manner the guarantees. With respect, Mr. President, to the personal situation of the accused -- I'm sorry, Mr. President, I need to return to one factor concerning the guarantees of the Federation which I forgot to mention. That is an issue which was raised by the Prosecution in its response to our motion for provisional release. There appears to have been a suggestion that because of the personal situation of the accused, namely that he is the highest-level accused to be indicted before the Tribunal, that this would make a difference in the weight to be attributed to the guarantees provided by the Federation. We have replied to this argument, Your Honour, and we have explained that in our view, first, General Delic is no longer the commander of the army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. For the past five years he has been a civilian and even if he was in that capacity, the Minister of Justice of the Federation will be able to highlight that this does not make a difference in terms of their ability to react in case there would be any attempt not to abide by an order of this Chamber. I move on quickly, Mr. President, to the personal situation of Rasim Delic. I underline once again his voluntary surrender; the fact that he has provided an undertaking which Your Honours have on the record; the fact that since the war and since he has left his position as commander of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or the army of the Federation, he has undertaken studies leading to the degree of Ph.D. or Doctor of Philosophy, which he has obtained in December of 2004. General Delic has published a number of books and he is a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina who is well-established in his community and, with all evidence that we can find, is a person who is deeply committed to remaining in this community. The family situation of Rasim Delic is another factor that shows that he would not be the type of person to escape or not to respect the provisional -- sorry, to -- not respect the conditions imposed along with his provisional release. He, with his family lives in Visoko, his two sons live in Visoko and all of his close relatives are also living in the territory of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is important, Mr. President, because as highlighted in our motion, two of his closest relatives are in a position where they cannot travel to go and see General Delic if he was limited to staying in Visoko which is his home address. One last item I wish to highlight concerning specifically Rasim Delic is the issue of cooperation. Rasim Delic, Mr. President, did cooperate with this Tribunal when he held the position of commander of the army, or at least there is absolutely no indication that the army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina ever held back on any request from this Tribunal. Rasim Delic has cooperated with this Tribunal when he was required to give a witness statement and to meet with the investigators of the Office of the Prosecution when dealing with the case of the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic. Before being indicted, it was publicly known in Bosnia and Herzegovina that Rasim Delic was willing to cooperate with the International Tribunal and to place himself at the disposal of the Tribunal, whether as a witness, as an accused, or in any other capacity. For all these reasons, Mr. President, we believe that the conditions that Rule 65 have been met, that there are no reasons not to respect his life [sic] to liberty, and we respectfully ask this Trial Chamber to grant provisional release until the beginning of the trial phase of the proceedings. I end my submissions, Mr. President, by a few words on the terms and conditions which could be imposed by this Trial Chamber should it be of the view that it is appropriate to grant provisional release to Mr. Delic. These conditions have been proposed already in our motion and I will not go over these conditions again. However, I highlight the fact that there is one condition which is required -- which is requested, Mr. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. President, and that is that the accused be entitled to move freely on the territory of the Federation. This is the type of conditions which has been granted to other accused in the past including the accused Sefer Halilovic, who was then authorised to remain on the territory of the Federation. This issue has been discussed with the government of the Federation and in their view, and the Minister of Justice will be able to further highlight this issue, this does not represent a problem, and the guarantees they offer of course stand for the complete territory of the Federation. With respect to all other conditions, Mr. President, the accused Rasim Delic is, respectfully, very flexible. The reason why he would like to be able to travel on the territory of the Federation is twofold: first, to visit his close relatives, namely his brothers who are both not in a position to visit him if he stays in his place of residence in Visoko; and the second is that Rasim Delic is expected to publish his fourth book in a relatively short period of time and it is expected that on this occasion, there will be a promotion tour for his book, like there was for the three previous books. In such a situation, Mr. President, the accused would travel to the main cities of the federation where he would participate in official promotion activities for his book. This sums up my submissions on behalf of the accused Rasim Delic, and it will be my pleasure, Mr. President, Your Honours, to answer any questions you may have with respect to the submissions, whether in writing or my oral submissions this afternoon. Equally, Mr. Delic is here. He has provided an undertaking, as I've mentioned earlier, and he is certainly willing to confirm this undertaking and answer any questions Your Honours might have with respect to his commitment to return for trial and not to pose any danger for anybody involved or any victims or witnesses. Those are my submissions. I'm grateful, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, you gave us, I think one medical report, is that right? For Ramiz.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. There is one medical report for the closest brother of Rasim Delic, and this medical report indicates that this person is unable to travel and that this person is -- also the information provided is that this person has regular contacts with the accused, Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where do I see that he is unable to travel?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I look at the medical report is found in Annex -- I refer you, Your Honour, to -- Annex G, annex golf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this is the brother of General Delic, and in this document in Annex G or golf, it is stated that there is an impossibility to travel. If I may just refer to Annex golf. Your Honour, I have the form here and we have the documents, and it's Annex J, and not -- Juliet and not golf, I'm sorry -- where we have a report. And according to the information provided in this report, it is stated that duties at the working place for which the evaluation of working capability is given, and health-related information, we have here what type --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I just wanted to know where it said he couldn't travel. That was all. I know that he is limbless and I know that he at one time suffered from another condition, but it seemed that these did not stop him from working, and I just wondered if there was a clear statement that he could not travel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, of course, the ability to travel is something that nowadays is more easy but this gentleman, of course, has both legs amputated to the knees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But he was working after that, I think; is that right? That didn't stop him from working. Or have I misunderstood?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That didn't stop him working in a shop where he is. The short answer to your question is there is no specific comment which says "unable to travel." However, there is, where we have a paragraph 8, and it says here that "opinion of the need for permanent help and care by other persons" or "need for permanent help by other person," and it says, "permanent help and care is necessary by the other person for carrying out basic life necessities." And this started on the 4th of April 1998. Now, again, if your question is does it say specifically unable to travel, no; but it certainly makes it much more difficult and -- to say almost impossible, in the absence of a statement, and it is certainly in our view a submission which would justify Mr. Delic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Presumably, if he were to travel the person who is the caregiver would also have to travel with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This appears to be indeed the case, Mr. President. That person could travel with the assistance of someone giving the care.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not could, but would have to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would have to, yes, indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the subject area of Mr. Delic's Ph.D.?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The subject was related with the war in Bosnia. The exact title is in the motion and it deals with the security situation. The title of his Ph.D. is as follows: "Creation, development and the role of the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And as was provided to Your Honours in our written submissions, this diploma for Doctor of Defence and Security Sciences has been awarded to Mr. Delic on the 20th of December 2004 at the Faculty of Political Sciences in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, if you could give us the names of those accused who are provisionally released and also allowed to move freely inside his national border, other than Mr. Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I believe there are no others, Your Honour. I believe Rasim -- that Sefer Halilovic was the only one to be granted such a condition. In my respectful submission, Your Honour, the facts of this case, the guarantees provided and the type of individual that is Mr. Delic, he is now a man of science, as he likes to call himself. He wears -- I'm not sure if this is the right word, but he is called Doctor. He is in scientific circles, and all the conditions in this case, all the facts of this case, make it that for him to be able to travel on the complete territory of the Federation, both for his professional, scientific activities, and for his personal family reason, would be both justified and would be appropriate in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My next question is how far or near is Sarajevo from Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Visoko is very close to Sarajevo. As indicated in our written submissions, Mr. Delic has an apartment in Sarajevo and his family house is in Visoko. The distance between the two is, I guess, it's less than 25 kilometres. And for some people, Visoko is actually considered as being part of Sarajevo, although on the terms it is not part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank, Your Honours. The Prosecution's position is very clearly set forth in her response of 13th of April 2005. The Prosecutor's position is that Rule 65(B) as Mr. Bourgon has indicated does set forth two general conditions, including the fact that the Trial Chamber must satisfy itself that the accused will appear for trial. The jurisprudence of this Tribunal, including the jurisprudence of the Appeals Chamber, sets forth a number of factors that a Chamber may consider in satisfying itself that an accused will in fact appear for trial. The Prosecutor's position as set forth in our response is clearly that several of those factors are of particular importance in this case. We have made reference to those, or the Prosecutor has made reference to those in her response. They include the senior position of the accused and the relationship between that senior position and the willingness of state authorities to arrest the accused in the event he failed to respond to a summons to reappear before this Tribunal; the serious nature of the charges that the accused faces, with the attendant possibility of a very serious sentence of confinement in the event he were to be convicted of those charges; the fact that although the accused did provide a statement in 2001 concerning a different case, the accused -- the Prosecutor's view does not -- has not substantially cooperated with the Tribunal; and of course, the argument that in light of the fact that the case has not currently docketed is a factor that the Prosecutor believes the Trial Chamber should consider in terms of the provisional release decision which the Trial Chamber must make. Again, Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecutor's position is quite straightforward and quite simple. It is set forth in our response and I will be happy to answer any questions that the Trial Chamber might have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, there is a suggestion -- or more than a suggestion, a statement in the application for provisional release that the Prosecution had indicated they would not oppose it. Are you able to enlighten us any further on how that impression may have been created in the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, or Your Honour, I believe that that, in light of the corrigendum filed by the Defence, has been explained. I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. do believe that there was in fact a misunderstanding that was the result of a discussion between Mr. Bourgon and myself in the recess of a different trial proceeding that we are both involved in. Our position is quite clear, that it's the Prosecutor or attorneys on behalf of the Prosecution in terms of filing written responses or in terms of oral responses before the Trial Chamber whereby the Prosecutor makes her position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you accept, then, that what is quoted as the exchange in the corrigendum is accurate?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my recollection of that discussion was along the lines that the Prosecution would make a decision based on the position to be taken at the time the Defence or the accused made an application. I do not recall at any point in time indicating that the Prosecution would not oppose or would not take a position with respect to provisional release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The actual words attributed are "the Prosecution is not likely to oppose the motion."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I don't recall, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon is on his feet, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I intervene at this time? I understand that this is an issue for which I would like to take the full responsibility. This was a conversation between my colleague and I. I may have misunderstood what the situation was. It was made clear to me that what would happen is that it was to be evaluated on the basis of the written submissions, and it was my mistake not to take the motion, to show it to my colleague before so that he could read it and say, yes, go ahead. I've done this in other cases and this time I have not, and I take the responsibility for such a move, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. That clarifies that matter. And thank you for being so forthright. Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When do you think this trial can start, can get started?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the workings of the scheduling committee of this Tribunal, as I'm sure you're aware, are such that the case is not currently on the docket. It would seem that it's not likely to go to trial until perhaps the second half of 2007, although, of course, there are a number of factors that impact upon the scheduling of cases. The Prosecution would anticipate this that this trial would last somewhere between most likely 12 and 18 months. Your Honour might be referring to the Prosecutor's position as set forth in paragraph 4 of the response. And the Prosecutor's position in this regard, Your Honour, is simply that as the Tribunal moves closer to its anticipated completion date with respect to trials, in the event an accused were not to voluntarily resurrender upon being ordered to do so, and were in effect to go into hiding or to go on the run, that the state or authorities concerned would have a relatively short window in which to bring the accused back within the custody of the International Tribunal and consequently we would perhaps be facing potential problems with respect to actually commencing trials under those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, you say that it is not likely to go to trial until perhaps the second half of 2007. We are now in the first half of 2005. So that your own -- on your own assessment, were the accused not to be granted provisional release, he would be in detention for about two and a half years, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President. There are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you a little bit embarrassed by that, by having to make that submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution stands by the response as filed on the 14th of April 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm a little bit embarrassed to be part of a system where I would have to acknowledge that. I know that other accused have spent two and a half years or even more in detention, but I don't think that that was ever acknowledged at the beginning of the case as it is now. But I think that's a fairly significant factor. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Ms. Borjana, Ms. Kristo, rather, the Minister of Justice of the Federation, I don't know whether you have any comments that you would wish to make, particularly in relation to the guarantees.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRISTO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honours, on behalf of the government of the Federation. As Minister of Justice, I now orally submit the guarantees which the government of the Federation has already provided in writing to the Chamber, and to the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia. On behalf of the federation government, I wish to express once again and emphasise our commitment to cooperating with the Tribunal, with this Trial Chamber in particular, and in expressing this commitment, I wish to put forward the clear standpoint of the government, that we are willing to fulfil all the conditions imposed upon us by this Chamber and the International Tribunal and we are willing to respond to any instructions. Should Rasim Delic be granted provisional release and permitted to live on the territory of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I reiterate the guarantees of the government that he will appear for his trial, that he will not be a danger to any victim or witness, and that he will fulfil any other conditions imposed by this Chamber. Let me reiterate, Your Honours, that we have already given oral guarantees before this and other Trial Chambers and I hope that you have been able to assure yourselves of our readiness to comply. I am ready to answer any questions Your Honours might have for me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Kristo. We don't have any questions of you. Thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRISTO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there any other matter that any party wishes to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave I would like simply to make a quick reply on one issue and that is the issue of the request for Mr. Delic to be able to travel on the territory of the Federation. I would simply highlight our submission in our written pleadings and that deals with the rule of proportionality. And I think that this is highlighted that the conclusion is that of course, if it is sufficient to use a more lenient measure, it must be applied. In this case, in light of the guarantees provided by the government, in light of the need, both to ensure that the accused will come back but also that he can have a living, I would -- it would be our submission, Mr. President, that such a condition, to be able to travel on the territory of the Federation, which could be accompanied by having the need to warn the authorities a certain number of days in advance, would be a proportional measure in the circumstances. And finally, Mr. President, I did not answer all the submissions of the Prosecution in my oral argument. We did so in writing, but there is only one that I think is important at this time, and it's the idea of cooperation. We highlighted the fact in our reply that there should not be -- the fact that the accused did not give a statement after being indicted, he should not be -- this should not be held against him in the sense of obtaining provisional release. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, just so you're in no doubt about it, the thing that made me ask about the travel arrangements or the ability to travel was to see that there was a very good reason for allowing that, because your other basis for requesting freedom to travel concerns me greatly, that is to engage in a public -- a publicity campaign, and I have a question in my own mind about whether that's an appropriate thing to be done during a period on provisional release. So it was more to establish if there was another basis for travel, and the health basis I think has been made out on the face of it, but it may be that there should be other conditions about what can be done during these periods of travel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I think you are quite right. These are quite valid concerns that you ever and I've discussed this issue with Mr. Delic this morning. What we can say and what we tried to put in our submission is that that even though we talk about promotion, these are scientific activities. These are not propaganda. These are not communication. These are not -- these are ideas where Mr. Delic has, as a man of science, and as a holder of a Ph.D. degree, he entertains relationships and this would allow him to continue doing so. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's a kind of literary endeavour. There being no other matter, this hearing is adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.45 p.m.
